passages.passage_text: Opponent-process theory proposes that, after three cone types transduce light, downstream neurons encode color along red-green, blue-yellow, and black-white axes. A researcher tested whether afterimage strength reflects fatigue in these opponent channels. Thirty participants with normal trichromatic vision and 30 participants with deuteranopia (absent medium-wavelength cones) fixated a saturated red disk or, on a separate day, a saturated blue disk for 10, 30, or 60 s. Immediately afterward, each viewed a uniform white field and pressed a key when the afterimage faded. Participants also named the dominant hue of the afterimage. Viewing distance, disk luminance, and room lighting were held constant, and the order of colors was counterbalanced. Mean afterimage durations appear in Table 1 and Figure 1. All trichromats reported a greenish afterimage after red adaptation and a yellowish afterimage after blue adaptation. Deuteranopes reported a yellowish afterimage after blue adaptation but described only a faint, colorless dark patch after red adaptation.
passages.table_data:
| Adaptation time (s) | Trichromats, red (s) | Trichromats, blue (s) | Deuteranopes, red (s) | Deuteranopes, blue (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 3.8 | 3.5 | 1.2 | 3.3 |
| 30 | 7.9 | 7.4 | 2.0 | 7.1 |
| 60 | 11.6 | 10.9 | 2.6 | 10.5 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean afterimage duration by adaptation time

questions.stem: The greenish afterimage reported by trichromats after red adaptation is best explained by which process?

options.A: Long-wavelength cones permanently lose their photopigment during adaptation, so short-wavelength cones alone signal green once the white field appears
options.B: Feature detectors in primary visual cortex for red habituate fully, so the blue-yellow channel takes over and labels the white field as green
options.C: Prolonged stimulation fatigues the red-signaling side of the red-green channel, so the green-signaling side dominates when the white field appears
options.D: Rods saturate during red fixation and send a green-labeled signal to visual cortex through the dorsal stream when the white field is shown

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Prolonged stimulation fatigues the red-signaling side of the red-green channel, so the green-signaling side dominates when the white field appears - sustained red input fatigues one pole of the red-green opponent channel, producing a rebound toward green on a neutral field. Why the others are wrong: A) Pigment bleaching is temporary and cannot by itself generate a green hue; the complementary color arises from opponent channels. B) The blue-yellow channel signals blue or yellow, not green; green belongs to the red-green axis. D) Rods do not mediate color, and the dorsal stream is not a color pathway.
questions.trap: Attributing the afterimage to photopigment bleaching alone rather than to rebound in an opponent channel.

questions.stem: Compared with trichromats, deuteranopes showed much shorter afterimages after red adaptation but nearly normal afterimages after blue adaptation. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?

options.A: Deuteranopes have fewer rods than trichromats, so the dark-adapted system contributes weaker afterimages for long-wavelength stimuli only
options.B: Without short-wavelength cones the blue-yellow channel receives little input, so afterimages of every hue are shortened in deuteranopes
options.C: Without medium-wavelength cones the red-green channel receives little differential input and fatigues weakly, while the blue-yellow channel is intact
options.D: Deuteranopes have impaired blue-yellow processing, which is why their blue afterimages were reduced relative to trichromats in Table 1

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Without medium-wavelength cones the red-green channel receives little differential input and fatigues weakly, while the blue-yellow channel is intact - the deficit is specific to the red-green axis, whereas blue-yellow input from S cones is preserved. Why the others are wrong: A) Rods are not color-specific and would not selectively affect red afterimages. B) Deuteranopia involves M cones; blue afterimages were normal, contradicting a blue-yellow deficit. D) Table 1 shows blue durations for deuteranopes (3.3, 7.1, 10.5 s) nearly equal to trichromats, so this misreads the data.
questions.trap: Confusing which cone type is missing in deuteranopia and which opponent channel it affects.

questions.stem: In trichromats, by how much did afterimage duration after red adaptation increase between 10 s and 60 s of adaptation?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) 7.8 s - 11.6 s minus 3.8 s equals 7.8 s. Why the others are wrong: A) This is roughly the ratio 11.6/3.8, not the difference. C) This is the increase for the blue series (10.9 - 3.5), not red. D) This is the 60 s value itself, not the increase.
questions.trap: Reading the wrong series or reporting a ratio instead of a difference.

questions.stem: Which finding is most difficult to explain with a purely trichromatic account and best supports opponent-process coding?

options.A: Trichromats and deuteranopes both perceive the white field as colorless once the afterimage has completely faded away
options.B: Deuteranopes show weaker red-green discrimination than trichromats, as expected when one of three cone classes is missing
options.C: Afterimage duration increases as adaptation time increases for every group tested, from 10 s through 60 s of fixation
options.D: Afterimages appear in complementary hues, green after red and yellow after blue, rather than in the hue of the adapting stimulus

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Afterimages appear in complementary hues, green after red and yellow after blue, rather than in the hue of the adapting stimulus - cone responses alone predict reduced sensitivity, not a complementary hue; paired opposing channels explain the rebound. Why the others are wrong: A) Perceiving white as colorless does not distinguish between the theories. B) Reduced discrimination with a missing cone class is exactly what trichromacy predicts. C) Longer adaptation producing stronger fatigue is compatible with either theory.
questions.trap: Choosing a result that fits both theories equally well.

questions.stem: Opponent processing of color first appears at which level of the visual pathway?

options.A: The outer segments of cones, where three photopigments are already arranged in opposing excitatory and inhibitory pairs
options.B: Retinal ganglion cells and the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
options.C: The medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, which relays color signals toward the primary visual cortex for integration
options.D: The superior colliculus, which compares cone outputs to direct eye movements toward objects of a particular hue

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Retinal ganglion cells and the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus - cone signals are recombined into opponent channels in ganglion cells and LGN neurons, before cortical processing. Why the others are wrong: A) Cones are trichromatic; opponency arises when their outputs are compared downstream. C) The MGN is part of the auditory pathway. D) The superior colliculus guides orienting, not color opponency.
questions.trap: Assuming opponent coding occurs in photoreceptors because the theory is often presented alongside cone types.

passages.passage_text: The Stroop task requires participants to name the ink color of a stimulus while ignoring its meaning. Forty-eight undergraduates completed three trial types on a computer: congruent (the word BLUE printed in blue ink), neutral (a row of Xs printed in blue ink), and incongruent (the word RED printed in blue ink). Participants pressed one of four keys to report ink color, and response time (RT) and errors were recorded for each trial. In Part 1, congruent, neutral, and incongruent trials appeared equally often. In Part 2, researchers varied the proportion of incongruent trials across separate blocks that contained only congruent and incongruent trials: 25% incongruent in one block and 75% incongruent in another. Block order was counterbalanced across participants, and each block contained 120 trials. The researchers hypothesized that participants would adjust their level of attentional control according to how likely conflict was. Mean RTs and error rates are shown in Table 1.
passages.table_data:
| Block | Congruent RT (ms) | Neutral RT (ms) | Incongruent RT (ms) | Incongruent errors (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Part 1 (equal mix) | 612 | 655 | 782 | 9 |
| 25% incongruent | 598 | not presented | 801 | 11 |
| 75% incongruent | 640 | not presented | 745 | 6 |

questions.stem: In Part 1, what was the interference effect, defined as incongruent RT minus neutral RT?

options.A: 127 ms
options.B: 203 ms
options.C: 43 ms
options.D: 170 ms

questions.explanation: Correct: A) 127 ms - 782 ms minus 655 ms equals 127 ms. Why the others are wrong: B) This is the 25% block difference (801 - 598), a different block and baseline. C) This is neutral minus congruent (655 - 612), the facilitation effect. D) This subtracts the congruent RT (782 - 612), which includes facilitation, not interference alone.
questions.trap: Using the congruent condition as the baseline when the question specifies neutral.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for slower and less accurate responses on incongruent trials?

options.A: Word reading is a highly practiced, automatic process that competes with the slower, controlled process of naming ink color
options.B: Color naming is the automatic process and word reading is the controlled one, so the word must be inhibited before the ink color is named
options.C: Holding four response keys in working memory exceeds capacity only on incongruent trials, producing errors unrelated to the printed words
options.D: Conflicting words physically mask the ink color, so participants cannot perceive the color on incongruent trials without extra viewing time

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Word reading is a highly practiced, automatic process that competes with the slower, controlled process of naming ink color - the automatic word response conflicts with the task-relevant color response and must be suppressed by selective attention. Why the others are wrong: B) The automaticity is reversed; reading is the more practiced response. C) The key mapping was identical across trial types, so memory load cannot explain the difference. D) Participants see the ink color clearly; the problem is response competition, not perception.
questions.trap: Reversing which process is automatic.

questions.stem: In Part 2, the interference effect (incongruent minus congruent RT) was smaller in the 75% incongruent block (105 ms) than in the 25% block (203 ms). What is the most reasonable interpretation?

options.A: Participants learned to ignore ink color and respond to the words instead, which removes conflict because the words are now the target
options.B: Frequent incongruent trials make word reading faster, so automatic reading becomes stronger and interference shrinks through added practice
options.C: When conflict is frequent, participants increase top-down attentional control, which reduces the influence of the irrelevant word
options.D: Participants in the 75% block were more fatigued, so slower congruent responses artificially compressed the difference between the conditions

questions.explanation: Correct: C) When conflict is frequent, participants increase top-down attentional control, which reduces the influence of the irrelevant word - conflict-adaptive control lowers interference where conflict is expected. Why the others are wrong: A) Responding to words would produce errors on the ink-color task; error rate actually fell to 6%. B) More practice reading words would strengthen, not weaken, the competing response. D) Fatigue is speculative and not supported; the congruent RT difference is small relative to the shift in incongruent RT.
questions.trap: Interpreting reduced interference as more automatic reading rather than more control.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of including the neutral condition in Part 1?

options.A: It controls for order effects by separating the congruent and incongruent trials so that participants cannot predict the next stimulus
options.B: It equalizes the number of trials per block so that error rates can be compared directly across the three conditions
options.C: It serves as a manipulation check showing that participants can see ink color when no word is present to distract them
options.D: It provides a baseline that separates speeding from congruent words (facilitation) from slowing caused by conflicting words (interference)

questions.explanation: Correct: D) It provides a baseline that separates speeding from congruent words (facilitation) from slowing caused by conflicting words (interference) - comparing neutral with congruent and incongruent trials partitions the Stroop effect into two components. Why the others are wrong: A) Counterbalancing, not a neutral trial type, handles order effects. B) Trial counts are not the purpose of a neutral condition. C) A check on perception is not what the neutral baseline is for; it isolates facilitation versus interference.
questions.trap: Treating the neutral condition as a mere filler or perception check.

passages.passage_text: In the transactional model of stress, stress arises when a person appraises situational demands as exceeding available resources. Researchers tested whether changing appraisal alters the hormonal stress response. Sixty healthy adults were randomly assigned to a reappraisal group, who were told that physiological arousal before a public speech improves performance, or to a control group, who received no instruction. All participants prepared and delivered a 5-minute speech and completed mental arithmetic in front of a stern evaluation panel. Saliva samples were collected before the task (0 min) and 20, 40, and 60 min afterward, and cortisol was measured in nmol/L. Participants also rated perceived task demands and perceived coping resources; a resources-to-demands ratio above 1.0 was classified as a challenge appraisal and a ratio below 1.0 as a threat appraisal. Mean cortisol appears in Figure 1, and appraisal results appear in Table 1. Sampling occurred in the afternoon, when baseline cortisol is relatively stable.
passages.table_data:
| Group | n | Mean resources/demands ratio | Participants with threat appraisal (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reappraisal | 30 | 1.12 | 30 |
| Control | 30 | 0.78 | 70 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean salivary cortisol before and after the speech task

questions.stem: Which appraisal process was most directly altered by the instruction given to the reappraisal group?

options.A: Primary appraisal, because participants decided that the speech task was irrelevant to their well-being and therefore not worth evaluating
options.B: Neither appraisal process, because cortisol responses are driven only by the physical features of the stressor and not by interpretation
options.C: Primary appraisal, because participants judged the evaluation panel to be benign and therefore classified the situation as harmless
options.D: Secondary appraisal, because participants reinterpreted their arousal as a resource available for coping with the speech

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Secondary appraisal, because participants reinterpreted their arousal as a resource available for coping with the speech - secondary appraisal evaluates coping resources, and the instruction recast arousal as helpful. Why the others are wrong: A) The speech remained relevant; the instruction changed perceived resources, not relevance. B) The data show that interpretation altered cortisol, contradicting a purely physical account. C) Panel behavior was identical across groups, so primary appraisal of the situation was not what changed.
questions.trap: Mixing up primary appraisal (is it a threat?) with secondary appraisal (can I cope?).

questions.stem: Cortisol released in response to the speech task is the end product of which sequence?

options.A: Sympathetic neurons stimulate the thyroid, whose hormones then trigger cortisol secretion from the posterior pituitary gland
options.B: Hypothalamic CRH stimulates adrenal medullary release of epinephrine, which then triggers cortisol secretion from the anterior pituitary
options.C: Hypothalamic CRH stimulates pituitary ACTH release, which stimulates cortisol secretion from the adrenal cortex
options.D: Pituitary ACTH stimulates hypothalamic CRH release, which stimulates cortisol secretion from the adrenal medulla through sympathetic nerves

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Hypothalamic CRH stimulates pituitary ACTH release, which stimulates cortisol secretion from the adrenal cortex - this is the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Why the others are wrong: A) Thyroid hormones and the posterior pituitary are not part of the cortisol cascade. B) Epinephrine is a medullary catecholamine and the pituitary does not secrete cortisol. D) The order is reversed and cortisol comes from the cortex, not the medulla.
questions.trap: Confusing the adrenal cortex (cortisol) with the adrenal medulla (epinephrine).

questions.stem: Relative to baseline, how large was the 20-minute cortisol increase in the reappraisal group compared with the control group?

options.A: About half as large, roughly 3.2 versus 6.5 nmol/L
options.B: About three-quarters as large, roughly 4.9 versus 6.5 nmol/L
options.C: About twice as large, roughly 13.0 versus 6.5 nmol/L
options.D: Nearly identical, roughly 6.0 versus 6.5 nmol/L

questions.explanation: Correct: A) About half as large, roughly 3.2 versus 6.5 nmol/L - reappraisal rise 11.0 - 7.8 = 3.2; control rise 14.5 - 8.0 = 6.5; 3.2/6.5 is about 0.49. Why the others are wrong: B) This does not match the figure values; the rise was 3.2, not 4.9. C) This reverses the groups; the reappraisal group had the smaller rise. D) The groups differed clearly at 20 min (11.0 versus 14.5 nmol/L).
questions.trap: Comparing the raw 20-min values instead of the change from baseline.

questions.stem: Why does peak cortisol occur roughly 20 minutes after the stressor rather than immediately, as heart rate does?

options.A: Cortisol is stored in salivary glands and released only after the stressor ends, whereas heart rate is controlled by hormones in blood
options.B: The parasympathetic system initially suppresses cortisol for several minutes, whereas heart rate is unaffected by parasympathetic output
options.C: Participants anticipate the stressor and release cortisol before it begins, so the later peak reflects only measurement delay in the assay
options.D: The HPA axis relies on a slower hormonal cascade, whereas the sympathetic-adrenal medullary response acts within seconds through neural signaling

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The HPA axis relies on a slower hormonal cascade, whereas the sympathetic-adrenal medullary response acts within seconds through neural signaling - endocrine cascades and steroid secretion take minutes, while sympathetic neural activation is nearly immediate. Why the others are wrong: A) Cortisol is not stored in salivary glands; saliva only reflects blood levels. B) The parasympathetic system does not gate cortisol release this way, and it does affect heart rate. C) Baseline was low before the task, so there was no anticipatory peak; the delay is physiological.
questions.trap: Assuming all stress hormones act at the same speed.

passages.passage_text: Erikson proposed that adolescence centers on a crisis of identity versus role confusion, whereas Marcia operationalized identity with two dimensions: exploration of alternatives and commitment to chosen roles. Combining these yields four statuses: diffusion (low exploration, low commitment), foreclosure (low exploration, high commitment), moratorium (high exploration, low commitment), and achievement (high exploration, high commitment). Researchers surveyed two separate samples of 150 emerging adults each, one aged 18 to 20 and one aged 24 to 26, recruited from the same community. Participants completed structured interviews about occupation, values, and relationships, which trained raters coded into the four statuses. Participants also completed a 100-point well-being scale. Raters were blind to well-being scores, and interviews were conducted individually by researchers who did not know participants' ages in advance. Participants received a small payment, and all responses were anonymized before coding. Table 1 shows the percentage of each sample in each status and the mean well-being score for each status across both samples combined.
passages.table_data:
| Status | Age 18-20 (%) | Age 24-26 (%) | Mean well-being (0-100) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Diffusion | 24 | 14 | 52 |
| Foreclosure | 30 | 22 | 64 |
| Moratorium | 28 | 20 | 58 |
| Achievement | 18 | 44 | 74 |

questions.stem: According to Erikson, which psychosocial stage follows the identity versus role confusion stage?

options.A: Intimacy versus isolation, in which young adults seek close commitments to others
options.B: Integrity versus despair, in which older adults reflect on whether their lives have been meaningful and well spent
options.C: Industry versus inferiority, in which school-age children develop competence by mastering tasks valued by their society
options.D: Generativity versus stagnation, in which adults seek to guide and contribute to the next generation through work and family

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Intimacy versus isolation, in which young adults seek close commitments to others - intimacy versus isolation is the young-adult stage after adolescence. Why the others are wrong: B) This is the final stage of late adulthood. C) This precedes adolescence. D) This is the middle-adulthood stage, two stages later.
questions.trap: Mixing up the order of Erikson's eight stages.

questions.stem: How many participants in the 24-26 sample were classified as identity achievement?
questions.explanation: Correct: C) 66 - 44% of 150 is 66. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the percentage itself, not the number of participants. B) This is 18% of 150, the 18-20 achievement figure. D) This is 56% of 150, the combined share of the other three statuses.
questions.trap: Reporting the percentage instead of converting to a count, or using the wrong sample.

questions.stem: Which pattern in Table 1 is most consistent with identity development across emerging adulthood?

options.A: The share in moratorium rises with age because exploration increases, while the share in achievement remains below one quarter
options.B: Foreclosure becomes the most common status in the older sample because commitments are made without exploring other alternatives
options.C: The share in diffusion stays about the same in both samples, indicating that lack of exploration is a stable trait through the 20s
options.D: The share in identity achievement rises sharply while the shares in diffusion, foreclosure, and moratorium all decline

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The share in identity achievement rises sharply while the shares in diffusion, foreclosure, and moratorium all decline - achievement rose from 18% to 44% while each other status fell. Why the others are wrong: A) Moratorium fell from 28% to 20% and achievement reached 44%. B) Achievement, not foreclosure, was most common at ages 24-26. C) Diffusion dropped from 24% to 14%.
questions.trap: Assuming exploration status increases with age instead of resolving into commitment.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation on concluding from these data that identity achievement increases with age within individuals?

options.A: Both samples were recruited from the same community, so the results cannot be compared and a different design is required to compare ages
options.B: Different people were studied at each age, so group differences may reflect cohort effects rather than change; following the same people over time would address this
options.C: The well-being scale ranges from 0 to 100, which is too broad a range to detect differences among the four identity statuses
options.D: The interviews were coded by trained raters, so coding errors are unavoidable and would make any comparison of percentages meaningless

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Different people were studied at each age, so group differences may reflect cohort effects rather than change; following the same people over time would address this - a cross-sectional design confounds age with cohort. Why the others are wrong: A) Sampling from the same community helps comparability; it is not the limitation. C) A 100-point scale is adequate; the problem is the age comparison, not scale range. D) Rater coding with blinding is a strength; it does not prevent age comparisons.
questions.trap: Overlooking that cross-sectional samples confound age with cohort.

passages.passage_text: In the minimal group paradigm, people are divided into groups on trivial bases and then allocate resources. Sixty-six students were told they would join one of two groups. In the random condition, membership was decided by a coin toss; in the preference condition, by a purported preference for paintings by Klee or Kandinsky; and in the control condition, no group labels were used. Participants never met other members, were identified only by code numbers, and could not benefit personally from their allocations. Each participant divided 100 points between two anonymous recipients, one from the participant's own group and one from the other group (in the control condition, two unlabeled recipients). Allocations were made privately in booklets, and the scorer did not know each participant's condition. Participants then completed a 7-point group identification scale. Table 1 shows mean allocations with 22 participants per condition. Figure 1 shows mean in-group bias (points to in-group minus points to out-group) by identification score among all labeled participants.
passages.table_data:
| Condition | Mean points to in-group (or recipient A) | Mean points to out-group (or recipient B) |
|---|---|---|
| Random (coin toss) | 56.2 | 43.8 |
| Preference (Klee/Kandinsky) | 58.1 | 41.9 |
| Control (no labels) | 50.3 | 49.7 |

graph.title: Figure 1. In-group bias by group identification score

questions.stem: What do the results of the random and preference conditions most directly demonstrate?

options.A: Participants allocate points according to personal gain, because they expect to receive resources from members of their own group later
options.B: Competition over scarce resources between groups is required before members will favor their own group over an outsider
options.C: Favoritism appears only when group membership reflects a meaningful shared preference, since coin-toss groups show no allocation bias
options.D: Mere categorization into groups, without contact, competition, or personal gain, is sufficient to produce in-group favoritism

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Mere categorization into groups, without contact, competition, or personal gain, is sufficient to produce in-group favoritism - favoritism appeared even though groups were arbitrary and anonymous. Why the others are wrong: A) Participants could not benefit personally, by design. B) Participants did not compete; favoritism arose anyway. C) The random condition also showed bias (56.2 versus 43.8).
questions.trap: Assuming intergroup conflict over resources is required for in-group bias.

questions.stem: What was the mean in-group bias in the preference condition?

options.A: 16.2 points
options.B: 8.1 points
options.C: 58.1 points
options.D: 12.4 points

questions.explanation: Correct: A) 16.2 points - 58.1 minus 41.9 is 16.2. Why the others are wrong: B) This is half of 16.2, which divides the difference by two. C) This is the in-group allocation itself, not the bias. D) This is the random condition bias (56.2 - 43.8).
questions.trap: Using one allocation rather than the difference between allocations.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the control condition?

options.A: To demonstrate that out-group members are always treated worse than in-group members regardless of how groups were created
options.B: To show that unequal allocation arises from group labels rather than from a general tendency to divide points unevenly between recipients
options.C: To increase the sample size of the study so that the allocation means in the labeled conditions can be estimated with more precision
options.D: To ensure that participants understand the instructions for dividing points because they are told which recipient belongs to their group

questions.explanation: Correct: B) To show that unequal allocation arises from group labels rather than from a general tendency to divide points unevenly between recipients - near-even allocation (50.3 versus 49.7) without labels gives the baseline. Why the others are wrong: A) The control shows no group-based difference, and it cannot show anything about all groups. C) The control does not contribute to estimates of the labeled conditions. D) Control participants received no group information; the purpose is a baseline.
questions.trap: Seeing a control condition as extra data rather than a baseline for comparison.

questions.stem: Social identity theory would explain the allocation pattern in which way?

options.A: People reduce cognitive dissonance after choosing a group, so they justify the choice by sending more points to recipients in the chosen group
options.B: People are born with an instinct to harm outsiders, so the allocation reflects an aggressive drive released by seeing any other group
options.C: People derive part of their self-esteem from group membership, so favoring the in-group raises the perceived worth of their own social identity
options.D: People imitate others they have seen rewarded for favoring their own group, so the allocation reflects social learning from observed models

questions.explanation: Correct: C) People derive part of their self-esteem from group membership, so favoring the in-group raises the perceived worth of their own social identity - this explains why identification tracks bias. Why the others are wrong: A) Dissonance reduction is a different theory and does not predict identification-related bias. B) Social identity theory is not an instinct theory; it concerns self-esteem and categorization. D) No models were observed in this study.
questions.trap: Attributing in-group favoritism to aggressive instinct or dissonance rather than self-esteem from group membership.

questions.stem: Using the endpoints of Figure 1, what is the approximate increase in in-group bias per one-point increase in identification score?

options.A: 4.5 points
options.B: 18 points
options.C: 3.6 points
options.D: 5.4 points

questions.explanation: Correct: A) 4.5 points - (19.0 - 1.0)/(6 - 2) is 4.5. Why the others are wrong: B) This is the total rise in bias, not the rate per unit of identification. C) This divides by 5 (the number of points on the x-axis) rather than 4 intervals. D) This is the increase from 5 to 6 of 5.0, not the average slope across the range.
questions.trap: Dividing by the wrong number of intervals or using the total rise.

passages.passage_text: The frustration-aggression hypothesis holds that blocking a goal increases the likelihood of aggression, and the weapons effect suggests that aggressive cues can prime aggressive responses. Eighty undergraduates were randomly assigned to cells of a 2 x 2 design (20 per cell). Frustration was manipulated by having participants work on puzzles under time pressure while a confederate repeatedly interrupted and insulted them; the puzzles were unsolvable (high frustration) or solvable (low frustration). Cue was manipulated by placing either a handgun or a badminton racquet on a nearby table, described as left over from another study. Participants then played a reaction-time game in which they could deliver noise blasts to the confederate and chose an intensity from 1 (very quiet) to 10 (very loud). Participants were told the confederate was another student, and the confederate wore headphones. No noise was actually delivered, and participants were fully debriefed afterward. Experimenters recording intensity were unaware of the cue condition. Mean intensity is shown in Table 1.
passages.table_data:
| Frustration | Handgun cue | Racquet cue |
|---|---|---|
| High | 6.8 | 5.1 |
| Low | 3.9 | 3.6 |

questions.stem: Averaged across both cues, how much higher was mean noise intensity under high frustration than under low frustration?

options.A: 1.5 points
options.B: 1.7 points
options.C: 2.9 points
options.D: 2.2 points

questions.explanation: Correct: D) 2.2 points - (6.8 + 5.1)/2 = 5.95; (3.9 + 3.6)/2 = 3.75; the difference is 2.2. Why the others are wrong: A) This compares only the racquet cells (5.1 - 3.6). B) This is the handgun-minus-racquet difference under high frustration. C) This compares only the handgun cells (6.8 - 3.9).
questions.trap: Comparing a single pair of cells instead of the marginal means.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the effect of the handgun cue?

options.A: The handgun raised intensity by about the same amount under both frustration levels, indicating a cue effect independent of anger
options.B: The handgun raised intensity by 2.9 points under high frustration, which shows the cue alone can account for the frustration effect
options.C: The handgun raised intensity by 1.7 points under high frustration but only 0.3 under low frustration, suggesting cues prime aggression mainly when anger is aroused
options.D: The handgun lowered intensity under low frustration because participants were inhibited by the weapon, which reversed the cue effect

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The handgun raised intensity by 1.7 points under high frustration but only 0.3 under low frustration, suggesting cues prime aggression mainly when anger is aroused - the cue effect depended on frustration level, an interaction. Why the others are wrong: A) The increases (1.7 versus 0.3) differ markedly. B) 2.9 is the high-versus-low frustration difference for handgun cells, not the cue effect. D) Intensity was slightly higher with the handgun (3.9 versus 3.6), not lower.
questions.trap: Describing main effects when the pattern is an interaction.

questions.stem: Which limitation applies most directly to the use of noise-blast intensity as the outcome measure?

options.A: The outcome was measured on a 10-point scale, which prevents any statistical comparison across the four cells of the design
options.B: Random assignment of participants to the four cells makes it impossible to compare mean intensity between the high and low frustration groups
options.C: A laboratory game rating may not capture real-world harmful aggression, which limits external validity of the conclusions
options.D: The confederate knew the hypothesis of the study, which guarantees that participants will deliver the maximum intensity in every cell

questions.explanation: Correct: C) A laboratory game rating may not capture real-world harmful aggression, which limits external validity of the conclusions - operational definitions of aggression in the lab may not generalize. Why the others are wrong: A) Ordinal-like scales are routinely analyzed this way; the issue is validity of the measure. B) Random assignment is what permits causal comparison. D) Nothing in the design implies this, and results varied across cells.
questions.trap: Confusing random assignment (internal validity) with external validity of an outcome measure.

questions.stem: Which finding would be most consistent with social learning theory rather than the frustration-aggression hypothesis?

options.A: Participants with higher baseline testosterone delivered louder blasts regardless of the condition to which they had been assigned
options.B: Participants who watched a model rewarded for delivering loud blasts then delivered louder blasts, even when they were not frustrated
options.C: Participants who were blocked from completing puzzles delivered louder blasts than participants who completed puzzles without interruption
options.D: Participants given an alternative outlet for frustration, such as a punching bag, subsequently delivered quieter blasts

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Participants who watched a model rewarded for delivering loud blasts then delivered louder blasts, even when they were not frustrated - aggression learned through observation and reinforcement occurs without frustration. Why the others are wrong: A) This implicates biological factors, not learning from models. C) This is the frustration-aggression prediction. D) This resembles catharsis, not social learning.
questions.trap: Choosing an observed correlate of aggression that is not about observational learning.

passages.passage_text: Sociologists treat healthcare as a social institution that organizes how societies define illness, distribute treatment, and train practitioners. A survey of 4,500 adults in a mid-sized metropolitan region compared access to care across household income levels. Respondents were grouped as low income (n = 1,500), middle income (n = 1,500), and high income (n = 1,500). Each reported whether they currently held health insurance, whether they had received a routine checkup in the previous 12 months, and whether they had delayed needed care in the previous year because of cost. Table 1 shows the results. Interviewers also asked how often respondents consulted a physician for conditions such as back pain or sleeplessness; the investigators noted that such experiences have increasingly been defined as medical problems over recent decades, and that physicians now hold primary authority over how they are labeled and treated. Respondents were selected by random-digit dialing, and the three income groups were similar in age and sex distribution.
passages.table_data:
| Income group | Insured (%) | Routine checkup in last 12 months (%) | Delayed care due to cost (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 78 | 52 | 24 |
| Middle | 90 | 66 | 11 |
| High | 96 | 78 | 4 |

questions.stem: Which sociological perspective most directly interprets the income gradient in Table 1?

options.A: Rational choice theory, because low-income adults weigh costs and benefits and voluntarily decide to forgo care that has little value
options.B: Functionalism, because health care efficiently allocates services to those who are most in need and thereby maintains social stability
options.C: Conflict theory, because differential access to care reflects an unequal distribution of resources and power in society
options.D: Symbolic interactionism, because patients and physicians construct shared meanings of illness during each individual clinical encounter

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Conflict theory, because differential access to care reflects an unequal distribution of resources and power in society - conflict theory emphasizes inequality in access to scarce social resources. Why the others are wrong: A) Cost delay reflects constrained resources, not freely chosen low valuation of care. B) Functionalism would not predict systematic disadvantage for low-income groups. D) This perspective concerns micro-level meanings, not the group-level gradient.
questions.trap: Selecting functionalism, which emphasizes stability, for a pattern of unequal access.

questions.stem: How many low-income respondents reported delaying care because of cost?
questions.explanation: Correct: A) 360 - 24% of 1,500 is 360. Why the others are wrong: B) This is 52% of 1,500, the checkup percentage. C) This is 78% of 1,500, the insured count. D) This is 11% of 1,500, the middle-income percentage.
questions.trap: Applying the wrong column or income group.

questions.stem: The investigators' observation about back pain and sleeplessness best illustrates which concept?

options.A: Anomie, in which rapid social change weakens norms and leaves individuals without clear guidance on acceptable behavior
options.B: Rationalization, in which social life becomes organized by efficiency, calculability, and impersonal rules over tradition
options.C: Medicalization, in which a human experience becomes defined and treated as a medical problem under professional authority
options.D: Deinstitutionalization, in which people formerly cared for in large facilities are moved to community settings with less supervision

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Medicalization, in which a human experience becomes defined and treated as a medical problem under professional authority - medicalization is the expansion of medical definitions to ordinary experiences. Why the others are wrong: A) Anomie concerns normlessness, not medical labeling. B) This is Weber's concept of bureaucratic organization, not defining conditions as medical. D) This concerns moving patients out of institutions.
questions.trap: Confusing medicalization with rationalization because both concern institutional authority.

questions.stem: Among low-income respondents, 78% were insured but 24% still delayed care for cost. What does this suggest?

options.A: Insurance coverage alone does not remove cost barriers such as deductibles and copayments, so access remains unequal
options.B: Surveys of delayed care are inherently invalid, since respondents cannot be expected to recall whether cost delayed care during the previous year
options.C: Insurance is unrelated to access to care, since delays occur at similar rates among insured and uninsured adults in every income group
options.D: Low-income respondents value preventive care less than higher-income respondents, which explains their lower checkup rates

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Insurance coverage alone does not remove cost barriers such as deductibles and copayments, so access remains unequal - being insured is not equivalent to affording care. Why the others are wrong: B) Self-report has limits, but nothing here shows it is invalid. C) The data do not separate insured from uninsured, so this overstates the data. D) Cost-related delay points to structural barriers, not valuation.
questions.trap: Equating insurance coverage with the ability to use care.

passages.passage_text: Demographic transition theory describes a shift from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as societies industrialize. Researchers compiled national statistics for one country over four decades: the percentage of the population living in urban areas, the total fertility rate (TFR; average number of births per woman), and the infant mortality rate (IMR; deaths per 1,000 live births). During this period, female secondary-school enrollment rose steadily, and wage labor in cities replaced farming as the main source of household income, so children shifted from being economic assets in farming households to costly dependents in cities. The crude death rate was already below 10 per 1,000 by 1980. Data are shown in Table 1, and Figure 1 plots TFR against percent urban for the four years. Replacement-level fertility in low-mortality countries is about 2.1. All figures come from census and vital registration records, and the four years were chosen at equal 20-year intervals.

graph.title: Figure 1. Total fertility rate by percent urban

questions.stem: Between 1980 and 2000, the country is best described as being in which stage of the demographic transition?

options.A: Stage 4, in which birth and death rates are both low and nearly equal, producing a stable and slowly changing population
options.B: Stage 1, in which both birth and death rates are high and population grows slowly because mortality offsets fertility
options.C: Stage 2, in which death rates fall sharply while birth rates remain high, producing the most rapid population growth
options.D: Stage 3, in which death rates are already low and birth rates are falling, so population growth is slowing

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Stage 3, in which death rates are already low and birth rates are falling, so population growth is slowing - death rate was low by 1980 and TFR fell from 5.1 to 3.3. Why the others are wrong: A) TFR of 3.3 is well above replacement, so growth was still substantial. B) Death rates were already low. C) Birth rates were declining by 2000.
questions.trap: Choosing stage 2 because death rates fell, ignoring the fall in births.

questions.stem: Which explanation best links rising urbanization to the decline in fertility shown here?

options.A: In cities children generate costs rather than farm labor, and education and wage work raise the opportunity cost of childbearing for women
options.B: Cities have higher death rates than rural areas, so parents have fewer children because fewer infants survive to be counted
options.C: Urban residents have less access to schooling, so women marry later and have fewer children because of lower educational attainment
options.D: Governments forced urban families to limit births, so the decline in TFR reflects coercion rather than any change in family economics

questions.explanation: Correct: A) In cities children generate costs rather than farm labor, and education and wage work raise the opportunity cost of childbearing for women - urban living and women's schooling reduce the economic value of children. Why the others are wrong: B) Infant mortality fell during this period. C) Female enrollment rose, and education typically lowers fertility. D) Nothing in the passage describes coercive policy.
questions.trap: Assuming lower fertility reflects higher mortality rather than changed incentives.

questions.stem: By approximately what percentage did TFR decrease from 1960 to 2020?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) 68% - (6.2 - 2.0)/6.2 is about 0.68. Why the others are wrong: A) This is not derived from the table values. C) This is the absolute decline (4.2 births) read as a percentage. D) This is the 2020 TFR as a proportion of 1960 (2.0/6.2).
questions.trap: Mixing an absolute change with a percentage change.

questions.stem: Even after TFR fell to 2.0, which factor best explains why the national population is still likely to grow for decades?

options.A: Urbanization itself raises the birth rate, so continued migration to cities raises TFR again in the years after 2020
options.B: Replacement-level fertility is 2.1, so a TFR of 2.0 is above replacement and directly guarantees that each generation is larger
options.C: Infant mortality is rising sharply, which increases the number of births needed to replace each family and keeps total births high
options.D: A large cohort of young women born during high-fertility years is entering childbearing age, producing population momentum

questions.explanation: Correct: D) A large cohort of young women born during high-fertility years is entering childbearing age, producing population momentum - age structure keeps births exceeding deaths for a time. Why the others are wrong: A) The data show urbanization accompanying lower fertility. B) 2.0 is slightly below 2.1. C) IMR fell to 12 per 1,000.
questions.trap: Assuming that near-replacement TFR means immediate population stability.

questions.stem: Using the 1960 and 2020 points in Figure 1, what is the approximate change in TFR for each 10-percentage-point increase in urban population?

options.A: A decrease of about 0.09 births per woman
options.B: A decrease of about 0.9 births per woman
options.C: A decrease of about 1.8 births per woman
options.D: A decrease of about 4.2 births per woman

questions.explanation: Correct: B) A decrease of about 0.9 births per woman - (2.0 - 6.2)/(68 - 22) is about -0.091 per point, or -0.9 per 10 points. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the change per single percentage point. C) This corresponds to a slope twice as steep as the data indicate. D) This is the total decline over the whole period.
questions.trap: Reporting per-point change or total change instead of per 10 points.

passages.passage_text: Residential segregation is often quantified with the dissimilarity index (D), which ranges from 0 (even distribution of two groups across neighborhoods) to 1 (complete separation). Researchers examined 40 U.S. metropolitan areas, divided them into tertiles of Black-white segregation, and computed asthma-related emergency department (ED) visits per 10,000 residents for Black and white residents. They also obtained the average poverty rate in majority-Black neighborhoods. All analyses were conducted at the level of the metropolitan area. Results are shown in Table 1, and Figure 1 plots the Black-white difference in ED visit rate against D for six metropolitan areas. The authors suggest that segregation concentrates poverty, older housing, and traffic-related air pollution in particular neighborhoods, affecting residents regardless of their individual behaviors. Rates were age-adjusted, and metropolitan areas were drawn from the same set of large cities in each tertile to keep population size comparable. The authors cautioned that the study was observational and that individual-level records were not available to them.
passages.table_data:
| Segregation tertile (mean D) | Black ED visits per 10,000 | White ED visits per 10,000 | Poverty in majority-Black neighborhoods (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low (0.32) | 28 | 17 | 19 |
| Medium (0.50) | 41 | 18 | 26 |
| High (0.68) | 63 | 19 | 34 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Black-white difference in asthma ED visit rate by segregation

questions.stem: A dissimilarity index of 0.68 indicates which of the following?

options.A: About 68% of one group would need to move to a different neighborhood for the two groups to be evenly distributed
options.B: The Black-white difference in asthma ED visits equals 0.68 times the rate among white residents in the same metropolitan area
options.C: Black residents have a poverty rate of 68% in the majority-Black neighborhoods of the metropolitan area on average
options.D: Black residents make up about 68% of the population of the metropolitan area and white residents make up the remaining 32%

questions.explanation: Correct: A) About 68% of one group would need to move to a different neighborhood for the two groups to be evenly distributed - D is the proportion of one group that would have to relocate for even distribution. Why the others are wrong: B) D is not a multiplier of ED rates. C) Poverty rate is a separate column. D) D measures distribution, not group share.
questions.trap: Interpreting D as a group's population share or as a rate.

questions.stem: In the high-segregation tertile, the Black asthma ED rate was approximately how many times the white rate?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) 3.3 - 63/19 is about 3.3. Why the others are wrong: A) This inverts the ratio (19/63). C) This is the low tertile ratio (28/17). D) This is the medium tertile ratio (41/18).
questions.trap: Using the wrong tertile or inverting the ratio.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best supports the authors' suggestion that segregation affects health independent of individual behavior?

options.A: Residents of segregated areas choose to smoke more often, which raises asthma risk through a behavioral pathway at the individual level
options.B: Segregation concentrates poverty and environmental hazards in particular neighborhoods, exposing all residents there to higher respiratory risk
options.C: Hospitals in segregated areas record more ED visits per person because they use broader diagnostic criteria for asthma than other hospitals
options.D: White residents in segregated areas are genetically less susceptible to asthma, which explains why their rates are flat across tertiles

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Segregation concentrates poverty and environmental hazards in particular neighborhoods, exposing all residents there to higher respiratory risk - neighborhood-level exposures act on residents irrespective of personal choices. Why the others are wrong: A) This is an individual-behavior explanation, contrary to the claim. C) No data indicate differences in diagnostic criteria. D) Genetic explanations are unsupported and do not fit the pattern.
questions.trap: Defaulting to individual behavior to explain health disparities.

questions.stem: Why can these results not show that an individual Black resident's asthma risk rises when that person lives in a more segregated area?

options.A: The data describe metropolitan areas, and relationships between aggregate measures may not hold for individuals, an ecological fallacy
options.B: Poverty is reported only for majority-Black neighborhoods, which proves that poverty has no relationship to asthma outcomes
options.C: Emergency department visits are measured per 10,000 residents, so the data cannot reflect any association with individual health
options.D: The tertiles contain unequal numbers of metropolitan areas, which invalidates any comparison of group means for individual residents

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The data describe metropolitan areas, and relationships between aggregate measures may not hold for individuals, an ecological fallacy - inference from group-level to individual-level data is unsafe. Why the others are wrong: B) Missing comparison data limit inference but do not prove no relationship. C) Rates per 10,000 are standard; the limit is aggregation level. D) Tertiles are by design nearly equal in size, and size does not address the individual-level issue.
questions.trap: Applying aggregate relationships directly to individuals.

passages.passage_text: A cohort study followed 1,000 adults aged 55 to 65 for five years to examine whether regular herbal tea drinking (at least one cup daily) is related to cardiovascular events (heart attack or stroke). At baseline, 500 participants reported drinking tea regularly and 500 did not. Researchers also recorded socioeconomic status (SES) as high or low and noted that high-SES participants were far more likely to drink tea. Participants were not randomized, and tea habits were self-reported once at baseline. Table 1 presents the number of participants, events, and five-year incidence overall and within SES strata. The risk ratio (RR) is the incidence among tea drinkers divided by the incidence among non-drinkers. The investigators also noted that, in general, low SES is associated with higher cardiovascular risk because of differences in diet, stress, and access to care. Participants with prior cardiovascular events were excluded at baseline, and follow-up was complete for all 1,000 participants.
passages.table_data:
| Stratum | Group | n | Events | Incidence (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All participants | Tea | 500 | 30 | 6.0 |
| All participants | No tea | 500 | 50 | 10.0 |
| High SES | Tea | 400 | 16 | 4.0 |
| High SES | No tea | 100 | 4 | 4.0 |
| Low SES | Tea | 100 | 14 | 14.0 |
| Low SES | No tea | 400 | 46 | 11.5 |

questions.stem: In this study, SES is best described as which of the following?

options.A: A confounder, because it is associated with both tea drinking and cardiovascular events without being a consequence of tea drinking
options.B: A mediator, because tea drinking causes higher SES, which in turn lowers the risk of cardiovascular events over the follow-up period
options.C: A dependent variable, because researchers measured it after cardiovascular events had occurred in each participant
options.D: An effect modifier only, because the risk ratio differs across strata and therefore SES cannot be associated with tea drinking

questions.explanation: Correct: A) A confounder, because it is associated with both tea drinking and cardiovascular events without being a consequence of tea drinking - SES relates to exposure and outcome and is not on the causal pathway. Why the others are wrong: B) Tea does not plausibly cause SES. C) SES was recorded at baseline and is not the outcome. D) SES clearly differs in tea use across groups.
questions.trap: Confusing a confounder with a mediator or an outcome.

questions.stem: What was the crude risk ratio for cardiovascular events comparing tea drinkers with non-drinkers?
questions.explanation: Correct: C) 0.60 - 6.0/10.0 equals 0.60. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the absolute risk reduction as a proportion of 10%, 1 - 0.60. B) This is the inverse (10.0/6.0). D) This is the risk ratio within the high-SES stratum, not the crude value.
questions.trap: Inverting the ratio or using the stratum-specific value.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the stratified results?

options.A: Tea drinking increases cardiovascular risk in all participants because the risk ratio in the low-SES stratum exceeds 1.0
options.B: SES has no relationship to cardiovascular events, because incidence among tea drinkers in the high-SES stratum equals that of non-drinkers
options.C: The apparent protective association is largely explained by confounding, since within the high-SES stratum incidence was equal and within the low-SES stratum it was not lower among tea drinkers
options.D: Tea drinking protects against cardiovascular events because the crude risk is lower among tea drinkers, and stratifying cannot change that finding

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The apparent protective association is largely explained by confounding, since within the high-SES stratum incidence was equal and within the low-SES stratum it was not lower among tea drinkers - stratum-specific RRs are 1.0 and about 1.2, compared with the crude 0.60. Why the others are wrong: A) The high-SES RR is 1.0 and the low-SES difference is not enough to claim a general harm. B) Incidence differs by SES (4.0% versus 11.5% to 14.0%), so SES is related to risk. D) Stratification can reveal confounding that reverses or removes a crude association.
questions.trap: Trusting the crude association without checking stratum-specific results.

questions.stem: Which design would best establish whether tea drinking causes a change in cardiovascular risk?

options.A: A larger cohort study with the same self-reported tea habits, because greater sample size removes bias from confounding variables
options.B: A randomized controlled trial in which participants are randomly assigned to drink tea or an alternative beverage and followed for events
options.C: A cross-sectional survey of tea habits and cardiovascular history at one time point, because it avoids the delay of a long follow-up
options.D: A case study of one heavy tea drinker followed in detail, because intensive observation can isolate the effect of a single exposure

questions.explanation: Correct: B) A randomized controlled trial in which participants are randomly assigned to drink tea or an alternative beverage and followed for events - random assignment balances both measured and unmeasured confounders across groups. Why the others are wrong: A) Sample size reduces random error, not confounding. C) Cross-sectional data cannot establish temporal order. D) A single case cannot isolate a causal effect.
questions.trap: Believing that larger observational samples remove confounding.

questions.stem: Even after stratifying by SES, why might the association between tea and cardiovascular events remain confounded?

options.A: Risk ratios cannot be calculated within strata, so the within-stratum comparisons are not valid for evaluating the role of SES
options.B: Unmeasured factors such as diet and exercise may differ between tea drinkers and non-drinkers within each SES stratum, leaving residual confounding
options.C: Stratification increases the correlation between the exposure and the outcome, so it adds bias to a previously unbiased comparison
options.D: Events were counted for only five years, so any difference in incidence is explained entirely by the length of the observation period

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Unmeasured factors such as diet and exercise may differ between tea drinkers and non-drinkers within each SES stratum, leaving residual confounding - stratifying by one variable adjusts only for that variable. Why the others are wrong: A) Risk ratios are routinely computed within strata, as in Table 1. C) Stratification does not add bias in this way. D) Follow-up length does not create a confounder.
questions.trap: Assuming that adjusting for one confounder eliminates all confounding.

discrete.stem: In a twin study of a personality trait, the correlation between monozygotic twins is 0.70 and between dizygotic twins reared together is 0.40. Using Falconer's formula (h2 = 2 x (rMZ - rDZ)), what is the estimated heritability?
discrete.explanation: Correct: B) 0.60 - 2 x (0.70 - 0.40) = 0.60. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the MZ correlation itself, which also includes shared environment. C) This is the difference rMZ - rDZ without doubling. D) This is the sum of the two correlations, which has no meaning here.
discrete.trap: Forgetting to double the difference in correlations.

discrete.stem: A patient with positive symptoms of schizophrenia, including hallucinations and delusions, improves after treatment with a drug that blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway. This response is most consistent with which hypothesis?

options.A: Positive symptoms reflect excess dopaminergic activity in mesolimbic circuits, which receptor blockade reduces
options.B: Positive symptoms reflect loss of acetylcholine neurons in the hippocampus, which dopamine receptor blockade compensates for by lowering inhibition
options.C: Positive symptoms reflect deficient serotonin reuptake in the prefrontal cortex, which receptor blockade of dopamine would not be expected to treat
options.D: Positive symptoms reflect excess GABA inhibition in the cerebellum, which dopamine receptor blockade relieves by increasing excitatory drive

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Positive symptoms reflect excess dopaminergic activity in mesolimbic circuits, which receptor blockade reduces - the dopamine hypothesis links positive symptoms to overactive mesolimbic dopamine. Why the others are wrong: B) Acetylcholine loss is associated with Alzheimer's disease. C) Serotonin reuptake deficiency is the monoamine hypothesis of depression, not this scenario. D) Nothing links schizophrenia positive symptoms to cerebellar GABA excess.
discrete.trap: Confusing the dopamine hypothesis with monoamine theories of depression.

discrete.stem: Dogs exposed to inescapable shocks later fail to jump a barrier to escape shocks they could easily avoid, while dogs without prior exposure escape readily. This outcome is most relevant to which explanation of depression?

options.A: Classical conditioning of fear, in which the barrier becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers an approach response toward the shock
options.B: Operant extinction, in which a response ceases because it is no longer reinforced when the dogs are tested on the barrier task
options.C: Opponent-process theory, in which a strong initial emotional reaction automatically produces an opposite reaction that grows stronger with repeated exposure
options.D: Learned helplessness, in which experiencing uncontrollable events leads to a belief that actions cannot change outcomes

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) Learned helplessness, in which experiencing uncontrollable events leads to a belief that actions cannot change outcomes - prior lack of control produced passivity even when escape became possible. Why the others are wrong: A) Conditioned fear would produce avoidance of the barrier, not passivity. B) Extinction requires prior reinforcement of the response being tested, which did not occur. C) This theory involves hedonic and counter-processes, not lack of control.
discrete.trap: Describing passivity as extinction rather than as generalized expectation of uncontrollability.

discrete.stem: A man collapses on a crowded subway platform. Seven bystanders are present and none helps for several minutes. Which concept best explains this?

options.A: Social loafing, in which individuals exert less effort on a collective task when their contributions cannot be identified individually
options.B: Group polarization, in which discussion among like-minded people shifts the group toward a more extreme version of its initial view
options.C: Diffusion of responsibility, in which each bystander assumes that someone else is more likely to intervene
options.D: Deindividuation, in which anonymity within a crowd leads people to lose self-awareness and act on impulses with fewer restraints

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) Diffusion of responsibility, in which each bystander assumes that someone else is more likely to intervene - larger groups reduce each person's felt personal responsibility. Why the others are wrong: A) This concerns reduced effort on group tasks, not helping in emergencies. B) No discussion or attitude shift is described. D) This explains disinhibited behavior, not helping failure.
discrete.trap: Choosing social loafing because it also involves reduced individual effort in groups.

discrete.stem: An experienced pianist performs a well-rehearsed piece better in front of an audience than when practicing alone, whereas a novice learning a new piece performs worse in front of the same audience. Which explanation is most consistent with these observations?

options.A: An audience lowers arousal, which weakens the dominant response, harming experts who rely on habit and helping novices who think carefully
options.B: An audience creates groupthink, which pressures experts to conform to the audience's expectations and novices to ignore them completely
options.C: An audience raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response, helping on well-learned tasks and hurting on novel tasks
options.D: An audience triggers diffusion of responsibility, which reduces effort for experts but increases effort for novices who need more practice

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) An audience raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response, helping on well-learned tasks and hurting on novel tasks - social facilitation depends on whether the dominant response is correct. Why the others are wrong: A) An audience raises rather than lowers arousal. B) Groupthink involves decision-making groups, not performance before spectators. D) Diffusion of responsibility does not predict opposite effects by expertise.
discrete.trap: Stating that audiences always improve or always impair performance.

discrete.stem: A manager notices that a company leadership team ignores dissenting opinions, privately doubts its plan but remains silent, and assumes that everyone agrees. Which phenomenon is most clearly shown?

options.A: Group polarization, in which discussion strengthens the average pre-existing view of members and produces an increasingly extreme position
options.B: Groupthink, marked by self-censorship and an illusion of unanimity that reduce critical evaluation of the plan
options.C: The fundamental attribution error, in which observers overestimate dispositional causes and underestimate situational causes of behavior
options.D: Social facilitation, in which the presence of others improves performance on simple tasks and impairs performance on complex tasks

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Groupthink, marked by self-censorship and an illusion of unanimity that reduce critical evaluation of the plan - these are classic symptoms of groupthink. Why the others are wrong: A) Polarization involves attitudes shifting toward an extreme, not silencing doubts. C) This concerns judging others' behavior, not suppressing dissent. D) This involves task performance, not decision-making.

discrete.stem: A viewer who is tired and uninterested in a product is persuaded by an advertisement featuring an attractive celebrity and an upbeat jingle, with little attention to the product's technical claims. According to the elaboration likelihood model, this is an example of which?

options.A: Peripheral-route processing, in which low motivation or ability leads to persuasion by superficial cues
options.B: Sensitization, in which repeated exposure to a strong stimulus produces progressively larger responses in the viewer
options.C: Cognitive dissonance reduction, in which the viewer changes the attitude to match a prior behavior that conflicts with it
options.D: Central-route processing, in which careful scrutiny of the product's technical claims leads to persuasion based on argument quality

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Peripheral-route processing, in which low motivation or ability leads to persuasion by superficial cues - attractiveness and jingle are peripheral cues. Why the others are wrong: B) Sensitization is a nonassociative learning concept, not a persuasion route. C) No behavior conflicting with the attitude is described. D) The viewer paid little attention to arguments.
discrete.trap: Assuming that persuasion by an attractive source involves careful message evaluation.

discrete.stem: In a classic study, participants performed a boring task, then were paid either $1 or $20 to tell the next participant it was enjoyable. Afterward, the $1 group rated the task as more enjoyable than the $20 group. Which theory best explains this result?

options.A: Self-serving bias, because participants in the $1 group attributed their success at the task to ability and its difficulty to external causes
options.B: Cognitive dissonance theory, because insufficient external justification leads people to change their attitude to match their behavior
options.C: Operant conditioning, because the larger payment reinforced the behavior and therefore increased the later liking of the task in the $20 group
options.D: Social facilitation, because telling another person about the task created an audience that increased arousal and improved ratings in all groups

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Cognitive dissonance theory, because insufficient external justification leads people to change their attitude to match their behavior - with only $1, the inconsistency is resolved by changing the attitude. Why the others are wrong: A) No attribution of success or failure is involved. C) The $20 group liked it less, opposite to a reinforcement account. D) Arousal from an audience would affect both groups similarly.
discrete.trap: Predicting that larger rewards produce more positive attitudes.

discrete.stem: A person new to a city initially startles at the sound of a nearby train every time it passes but, after several weeks, barely notices it. When a loud, unexpected siren sounds, the person again responds to the train sound strongly for a short time. The return of the response is best called?

options.A: Extinction, a decline in a conditioned response when the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus
options.B: Spontaneous recovery, the reappearance of an extinguished conditioned response after a rest interval without further training
options.C: Dishabituation, a restored response to a previously habituated stimulus after a new, strong stimulus
options.D: Stimulus generalization, a conditioned response to stimuli resembling the original conditioned stimulus but not identical to it

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) Dishabituation, a restored response to a previously habituated stimulus after a new, strong stimulus - habituation was followed by a recovery triggered by a novel stimulus. Why the others are wrong: A) No conditioned stimulus pairing is involved. B) This requires prior extinction of a conditioned response. D) The response returns to the same train sound, not a similar one.
discrete.trap: Applying classical conditioning terms to a nonassociative learning example.

discrete.stem: In a signal detection experiment, participants are told that a missed signal will cost them money but a false alarm will not. Assuming sensitivity (d') stays the same, how should the change in payoff affect responding?

options.A: Participants adopt a more liberal criterion, so both hits and false alarms increase
options.B: Participants adopt a more liberal criterion, so hits increase and false alarms decrease because the signal becomes physically more intense
options.C: Participants adopt a more conservative criterion, so both hits and false alarms decrease because they say yes only when very certain
options.D: Participants become more sensitive to the signal, so hits increase while false alarms decrease because discrimination improves

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Participants adopt a more liberal criterion, so both hits and false alarms increase - a lower criterion yields more 'yes' responses of both kinds. Why the others are wrong: B) Hits and false alarms move together with a criterion shift, and signal intensity is unchanged. C) A conservative criterion is favored when false alarms are costly. D) Sensitivity was held constant; payoffs shift bias, not d'.
discrete.trap: Confusing criterion shifts with changes in sensitivity.

discrete.stem: A person recalls the ten digits 5-5-5-0-1-2-3-4-5-6 correctly after seeing them once by grouping them as 555, 012, 3456. This strategy most directly demonstrates which concept?

options.A: Iconic memory, which briefly stores a detailed visual representation of the digits for a fraction of a second after they disappear
options.B: Rehearsal in long-term memory, which transfers each digit to permanent storage by repeating it silently over a long retention interval
options.C: Proactive interference, in which previously learned phone numbers disrupt recall of the newly presented sequence of digits
options.D: Chunking, which increases the amount of information held in working memory by organizing items into meaningful units

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) Chunking, which increases the amount of information held in working memory by organizing items into meaningful units - grouping digits expands effective capacity. Why the others are wrong: A) Iconic memory is a sensory store, not an organizing strategy. B) Chunking is a working-memory strategy, not long-term storage. C) Interference would impair, not improve, recall.
discrete.trap: Mistaking chunking for rote rehearsal into long-term memory.

discrete.stem: A patient who sustained damage to the prefrontal cortex in an accident becomes impulsive, irritable, and unable to plan, although memory and language are intact. This change is most consistent with disruption of which function?

options.A: Memory consolidation mediated by the hippocampus, which would be expected to produce severe anterograde amnesia in this patient
options.B: Executive control and emotional regulation mediated by frontal-lobe circuits
options.C: Visual-spatial processing mediated by the occipital lobe, which would be expected to produce blindness or impaired visual perception
options.D: Language comprehension mediated by Wernicke's area, which would be expected to produce fluent but meaningless speech in this patient

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Executive control and emotional regulation mediated by frontal-lobe circuits - frontal damage impairs planning, impulse control, and personality. Why the others are wrong: A) Memory is intact, and hippocampal damage mainly impairs new memories. C) The symptoms are behavioral, not visual. D) Language is intact.
discrete.trap: Attributing personality change to a region associated with memory or language.

discrete.stem: Students who successfully complete progressively harder practice problems report higher confidence in their ability to pass the course. According to Bandura, which source of self-efficacy does this most directly reflect?

options.A: Verbal persuasion, in which encouragement from teachers and peers raises belief in one's capabilities despite doubts
options.B: Physiological state, in which interpreting bodily arousal as excitement rather than anxiety improves perceived capability
options.C: Vicarious experience, in which watching similar others succeed raises one's own belief that the task can be accomplished
options.D: Mastery experiences, in which past successes build confidence in future performance

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) Mastery experiences, in which past successes build confidence in future performance - performing a task successfully is the strongest source of self-efficacy. Why the others are wrong: A) No encouragement is described. B) Arousal is not mentioned. C) This requires observing others, not personal success.
discrete.trap: Choosing verbal persuasion because teachers are present in the scenario.

discrete.stem: Over several decades, a country's leading causes of death shift from influenza, diarrhea, and tuberculosis to heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and life expectancy rises. Which concept best describes this shift?

options.A: The fertility transition, in which birth rates decline as urbanization and women's education increase across a population
options.B: The demographic dividend, in which a rising share of working-age people raises economic growth relative to dependent age groups
options.C: Medicalization, in which ordinary human experiences come to be defined and treated as medical conditions under professional authority
options.D: The epidemiologic transition, in which chronic and degenerative diseases replace infectious diseases as leading causes of death

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) The epidemiologic transition, in which chronic and degenerative diseases replace infectious diseases as leading causes of death - improved sanitation and medicine reduce infectious mortality. Why the others are wrong: A) This concerns births, not causes of death. B) This concerns age structure and economic growth. C) This concerns definitions of illness, not the cause-of-death pattern.
discrete.trap: Confusing the epidemiologic transition with the demographic transition.

discrete.stem: Country A's Gini coefficient rises from 0.35 to 0.45 over twenty years. What does this change indicate?

options.A: Income is becoming more equally distributed, since the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of perfect equality over time
options.B: The poverty rate has risen by 10 percentage points, since the Gini coefficient measures the share of people below the poverty line
options.C: The average income has increased by 10 percentage points, since the Gini coefficient measures growth in mean household income
options.D: Income is becoming more unequally distributed, since the Lorenz curve moves farther from the line of perfect equality

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) Income is becoming more unequally distributed, since the Lorenz curve moves farther from the line of perfect equality - a higher Gini means greater inequality. Why the others are wrong: A) A rise in Gini means the opposite. B) Gini does not measure the poverty rate. C) Gini measures distribution, not average income.
discrete.trap: Reading the Gini coefficient as average income or poverty rate.
